title: The Mongol Empire and the Making of the Modern World
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: The Mongols were both terrifying conquerors who massacred resisting cities and powerful integrators who connected Eurasia into a single network of exchange. The College Board titles this topic 'The Mongol Empire and the Making of the Modern World,' capturing how a wave of destruction helped build an interconnected world.

The yam was the Mongol relay messenger system, with stations roughly a day's ride apart stocked with fresh horses, food, and shelter. Riders swapped exhausted horses for fresh ones, allowing messages to cross thousands of miles of the empire in days rather than months.

Born Temujin around 1162, he united the feuding nomadic tribes of the Mongolian steppe and in 1206 was proclaimed Chinggis Khan (also spelled Genghis Khan), meaning 'universal ruler.' He died in 1227 after launching the conquests that built the empire.

The Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous land empire in human history, eventually stretching from the Pacific Ocean to Eastern Europe. It was built by Chinggis Khan and his successors beginning in the early 1200s.

The Mongols were peerless horsemen, raised in the saddle and able to ride and shoot composite bows at a gallop. Their mobility let them move armies with terrifying speed across vast distances, a key reason for their conquests.

Chinggis Khan reorganized his forces into a strict decimal system of units of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000. This broke up old tribal loyalties and welded soldiers into a disciplined, coordinated military machine.

The Mongols were quick learners who absorbed the technologies of the peoples they conquered, including adopting Chinese and Muslim siege engineers. This allowed nomadic armies to capture the walled cities they traditionally could not take.

The Mongols deliberately cultivated a reputation for massacre: cities that surrendered were often spared and taxed, while cities that resisted might be annihilated. This terror was a tool that persuaded many places to surrender without a fight, speeding conquest.

The Mongols practiced a pragmatic meritocracy, promoting commanders for skill and loyalty rather than birth and incorporating conquered soldiers into their ranks. They were also generally religiously tolerant of the faiths of conquered peoples.

After Chinggis Khan's death in 1227, the Mongol Empire was divided among his descendants and settled into four major khanates, regional Mongol states each ruling a different part of Eurasia. The khanates often acted independently and sometimes fought one another.

The Yuan Dynasty was the Mongol state in China, founded by Chinggis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan in 1271. Kublai ruled China as a Mongol emperor, using Chinese bureaucratic methods while keeping Mongols and foreigners, such as the visitor Marco Polo, privileged above the Chinese.

The Ilkhanate was the Mongol khanate ruling Persia and the Middle East. There Chinggis Khan's grandson Hulegu sacked Baghdad in 1258, killing the caliph and ending the Abbasid Caliphate; the Ilkhanate later converted to Islam.

In 1258 the Mongol leader Hulegu sacked Baghdad, killing the last Abbasid caliph and ending the Abbasid Caliphate after roughly 500 years. The destruction also ruined libraries and irrigation works in the region.
The Chagatai Khanate was the Mongol state ruling Central Asia, near the steppe heartland. It remained more nomadic in character than the other khanates.

The Golden Horde was the Mongol khanate that dominated Russia and the western steppe. It ruled the Russian principalities indirectly, leaving local princes in place but demanding heavy tribute, an era Russians remembered as the 'Mongol yoke.' It later converted to Islam.

The Mongols were conquerors but not cultural imperialists. Rather than imposing Mongol ways everywhere, they often adapted to and adopted local cultures: the Ilkhanate and Golden Horde converted to Islam, and the Yuan absorbed Chinese administrative practice.

The Pax Mongolica, or 'Mongol Peace,' was the period when a network of cooperating Mongol states secured the overland trade routes across Eurasia. Because a connected, prosperous empire generated taxes and tribute, the Mongols actively protected and promoted commerce, and the Silk Roads surged under their protection.

Valuing skill over origin, the Mongols relocated talented administrators, artisans, and scholars across thousands of miles to wherever they were useful. A Persian astronomer might advise in China, or Chinese engineers serve in Persia, making the empire a giant transmission belt for technology and ideas.

Chinese innovations including gunpowder weaponry diffused westward across the Mongol networks toward the Islamic world and Europe, where they would eventually transform warfare. The Mongols helped spread technologies that later enabled the gunpowder empires.

Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who journeyed to Kublai Khan's China during the Mongol era and brought back accounts that fascinated Europe. His travels were possible because the Mongol world was, for a few generations, open and connected.

Rabban Bar Sauma was a Christian monk born near Beijing who traveled all the way to Europe as a Mongol envoy. His journey illustrates the long-distance movement of people made possible by the connected Mongol world.

The Black Death spread across Eurasia along Mongol-secured trade routes. In 1346 a Mongol army besieging the Black Sea port of Caffa reportedly catapulted plague-infected corpses over the walls, and fleeing Genoese merchants then carried the disease into the Mediterranean, from which it ravaged the Middle East and Europe.

Evaluating the Mongols requires weighing both their destructiveness (the sack of Baghdad, massacres, spreading the plague) and their integrative role (the Pax Mongolica, circulating gunpowder and scholars, safer trade). The most sophisticated argument notes the two are connected: violently unifying vast territory created the single political space in which exchange could flourish.

The Mongols set off chain reactions across world history: ending the Abbasid Caliphate, transmitting gunpowder westward, ruling and shaping Russia through the Golden Horde, reviving the Silk Roads, and spreading the Black Death. They are a key example of how networks of exchange, more than single rulers or battles, drive world history.
